rows.headline: An introduction to the zodiac signs
rows.summary: Start with the sky itself. From where we stand on Earth, the Sun traces the same path across the year, and the Moon and planets never stray far from it. That path is called the ecliptic. Think of it as one road the whole solar system drives on, and everything in your chart as traffic on that road.
rows.body:
Start with the sky itself. From where we stand on Earth, the Sun traces the same path across the year, and the Moon and planets never stray far from it. That path is called the ecliptic. Think of it as one road the whole solar system drives on, and everything in your chart as traffic on that road.

The stars along that road don't move in relation to each other, which is why astronomers call them fixed. They were the original landmarks. The constellations scattered along the ecliptic gave the road its mile markers, and it takes the Sun a full year to pass all of them. Around the fifth century BCE, astrologers in Mesopotamia did something practical with that: they cut the circle into twelve equal slices of 30 degrees each. Those twelve slices are the zodiac signs.

This is the part that confuses people, so here it is plainly. A constellation is a cluster of actual stars, and the clusters are wildly uneven. Some sprawl. Some are crammed into a corner. A sign is a measurement. Twelve equal cuts of a circle, named after the constellations that once sat behind them. The signs share those names, but they are not the same thing.

Two zodiacs
Because the Earth wobbles slightly on its axis, the fixed stars appear to drift about one degree every 72 years. Over two thousand years, that adds up. The sign of Aries now sits roughly 24 degrees away from the constellation of the same name.

The ancients knew about the drift. That's why the tropical zodiac, the system most Western astrologers use, is anchored to something that doesn't move: the spring equinox, the day light and dark stand even. That moment is 0 degrees Aries, the start of the whole wheel. Everything else follows from it. The tropical zodiac is a calendar of the seasons, not a map of the stars.

The sidereal zodiac, used in most Indian astrology, shifts the signs to keep them lined up with the constellations instead. It's also made of twelve equal 30-degree cuts, so it's just as symbolic. Neither system is the true one. They answer different questions. TLDR Astro uses the tropical zodiac, in the Hellenistic tradition.

What a sign actually does
A sign is not a personality. It's a style. Planets are the actors in your chart, the parts of you that want things: the Sun wants to shine, the Moon wants to feel safe, Mars wants to act. A sign is the manner in which that wanting happens. Mars in Aries wants openly and immediately. Mars in Pisces wants quietly, and often on someone else's behalf.

So "I'm a Gemini" is a shorthand for "the Sun was in Gemini when I was born." It's real, and it's one placement out of many. The rest of the chart is where you actually live.

Four qualities define each sign, and every interpretation in this app is built out of them.

Polarity
The odd-numbered signs (Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, Aquarius) were called masculine in the older texts. The even-numbered ones (Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, Pisces) were called feminine. The language has moved on. We use diurnal and nocturnal, which is closer to what the tradition actually meant.

Diurnal signs are the fire and air signs. They move outward: faster, more direct, more visible.

Nocturnal signs are the earth and water signs. They move inward: slower, more receptive, more protective.

This isn't about gender or worth. It's about direction of travel.

Element
Four elements, three signs each. The ancients called these the triplicities.

Fire: Aries, Leo, Sagittarius. Fire is spirit, courage, and appetite for life. It rises, it spreads, and it needs air and room. Fire signs start things and inspire people. They burn out when there's nothing worth burning for.

Earth: Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn. Earth is the body, the material world, and everything you can count. Earth signs build, maintain, and finish. They are the reason anything actually gets done. They can also mistake what's solid for what's alive.

Air: Gemini, Libra, Aquarius. Air is thought, language, and connection. Air signs link people and ideas to each other, and they need to be able to talk it through. They can think about a feeling instead of having it.

Water: Cancer, Scorpio, Pisces. Water is feeling, memory, and attachment. Water signs read the room before anyone speaks and hold what other people can't carry. They can also absorb moods that were never theirs.

Modality
Three modalities, four signs each. Modality comes from the seasons, and it tells you how a sign moves.

Cardinal: Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn. These signs open a season. Each one begins at an equinox or a solstice. They initiate, lead, and set things in motion, and they can start more than they finish.

Fixed: Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius. These signs hold the middle of a season. They sustain, commit, and outlast. They're the ones still there when the excitement is gone, which is also why they stay too long.

Mutable: Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces. These signs close a season and hand it to the next one. They adapt, translate, and change shape. They can be hard to pin down, which is the same talent that makes them useful everywhere.

Element and modality together give you the sign. Fixed water is Scorpio: slow-building intensity, private, all or nothing. Cardinal fire is Aries: fast to start, hot, in need of a target.

Planetary rulership
Every sign is governed by a planet, and that planet is the sign's ruler. This is the backbone of traditional astrology, and it's the part most modern pop astrology skips.

TLDR Astro uses the seven visible planets, the ones ancient astrologers could see with their own eyes. Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto matter in a chart, and you'll find them on every sign page here. They do not rule signs. Mars rules Scorpio. Saturn rules Aquarius. Jupiter rules Pisces.

The Moon rules Cancer. The Moon governs the body, moods, and what makes you feel safe, and Cancer is the sign most attuned to what other people need before they say it.

The Sun rules Leo. The Sun is identity, vitality, and warmth. Leo is the sign that needs to be witnessed and knows how to light a room.

Mercury rules Gemini and Virgo. Mercury is thinking, language, and the handling of detail. In air-sign Gemini it's quick, curious, and interested in everything. In earth-sign Virgo it's precise, useful, and interested in what actually works.

Venus rules Taurus and Libra. Venus is love, pleasure, taste, and value. In earth-sign Taurus that's sensory: food, texture, money, the physical comfort of a life. In air-sign Libra it's relational: fairness, beauty, and the art of two people getting along.

Mars rules Aries and Scorpio. Mars is drive, courage, and conflict. In fire-sign Aries that heat is visible and immediate. In water-sign Scorpio it goes underground: patient, strategic, and impossible to read from the outside.

Jupiter rules Sagittarius and Pisces. Jupiter is growth, meaning, and faith that there's more. Fire-sign Sagittarius goes looking for it out in the world. Water-sign Pisces finds it inward, through imagination and compassion.

Saturn rules Capricorn and Aquarius. Saturn is structure, limits, and time. Earth-sign Capricorn applies that to building something that lasts. Air-sign Aquarius applies it to systems and ideas, which is why it can take an institution apart and reassemble it better.

Dignity: how a planet does in a sign
Some planets are more themselves in some signs than others. The tradition maps this in four positions, and you'll see them named throughout the app.

Domicile: the planet is home, in the sign it rules. It has everything it needs to work.

Exaltation: the planet is honored, a guest treated well. It shows its best face, sometimes more loudly than usual. The Sun is exalted in Aries, the Moon in Taurus, Mercury in Virgo, Venus in Pisces, Mars in Capricorn, Jupiter in Cancer, Saturn in Libra.

Detriment: the planet sits opposite its own sign, on unfamiliar ground. It still works. It just has to work in a manner that isn't native to it. Venus in Scorpio still loves. It loves in a way Venus wouldn't choose.

Fall: the planet sits opposite its exaltation, its hardest ground. This placement usually asks more of you and gives more back later than it does at the time.

Dignity is not a grade. A planet in fall is not a broken planet, and an exalted one is not a free pass. It describes conditions, and conditions are something you work with.

The six axes
Every sign has an opposite, and the two of them are one subject argued from both ends. A Full Moon always falls on one of these axes, which is why Full Moons feel like a choice between two true things.

- Aries / Libra: Self vs. Others. Independence and partnership.
- Taurus / Scorpio: Security vs. Transformation. What you keep and what you let go.
- Gemini / Sagittarius: Information vs. Wisdom. Details and the big picture.
- Cancer / Capricorn: Nurturing vs. Achievement. Home and the world.
- Leo / Aquarius: Personal Expression vs. Collective Good. Your voice and the group's.
- Virgo / Pisces: Precision vs. Flow. The fix and the surrender.

You have all twelve signs in your chart. Not one of them belongs to someone else.

Where to go next
Each sign has its own page here: what it means to have the Sun, Moon, rising sign, and every other planet or point in it. Start with your big three and read outward.

rows.headline: What is a birth chart?
rows.summary: A birth chart is a map of the sky from where you were standing at the moment you arrived. Not a picture of the stars in general. A picture of that sky, from that spot on Earth, at that minute. Same city, twenty minutes later, and the map is already different.
rows.body:
A birth chart is a map of the sky from where you were standing at the moment you arrived. Not a picture of the stars in general. A picture of that sky, from that spot on Earth, at that minute. Same city, twenty minutes later, and the map is already different.

That's why astrologers ask for three things: the date, the time, and the place. The date tells us where the planets were. The place tells us what the sky looked like from your particular patch of ground. The time is the one people underestimate, because the time sets the rising sign, and the rising sign sets the entire frame.

If you don't know your birth time, you can still read a chart. The planets are almost all in the right signs, and the ones that move fastest are the ones to hold loosely. What you lose is the houses and the exact Moon. It's worth asking a parent, checking your birth certificate, or requesting the long-form record from the state where you were born.

What's actually on the map
The chart is a circle, because the sky is a circle around you. That circle gets divided in two different ways at once, and every reading you'll ever do is some version of holding both at the same time.

The signs divide the circle by season. Twelve equal slices of 30 degrees, anchored to the spring equinox, telling you the manner in which something happens.

The houses divide the circle by your location and time of birth. Twelve areas of a life, telling you where it happens: your body, your money, your home, your work, your partnerships.

The planets are placed on that circle wherever they actually were. They're the what: the parts of you that want things.

Put those three together and you have a sentence. Mars (drive) in Cancer (protectively, indirectly) in the 10th house (your career and public role) reads as someone who fights for their work sideways, defends their people at the office, and hates a direct confrontation in front of an audience. Same Mars, different house, different life.

Planets, signs, houses
Here's the grammar, once, plainly.

A planet is a verb. The Sun shines. The Moon feels and needs. Mercury thinks and talks. Venus loves and values. Mars acts. Jupiter expands. Saturn limits and builds.

A sign is an adverb. Boldly. Slowly. Curiously. Tenderly. Precisely.

A house is a room. The place in your actual life where all that happens.

People get stuck on signs because signs are what pop astrology sells. But a planet's sign without its house is half a sentence. The house is where you live.

The angles
Four points on the chart are the corners of the map, and they're set by the birth time.

The Ascendant (rising sign) is the sign coming up over the eastern horizon when you were born. It's the start of your 1st house and, in whole-sign houses, the whole first house. It governs the body, the approach, the first impression, and it decides where every other house falls.

The Midheaven (MC) is the highest point, your public role and the direction you're visibly headed.

The Descendant (DC) sits opposite the Ascendant: partnership, and the qualities you meet in other people.

The Imum Coeli (IC) sits opposite the Midheaven, at the bottom of the chart: home, family, the private foundation nobody sees.

Rising and setting, high and low. The four angles are the load-bearing walls.

Whole-sign houses
There are several ways to divide houses, and TLDR Astro uses whole-sign houses, the system used in Hellenistic astrology and still standard in much of the world.

It works like this: whatever sign is rising becomes your entire 1st house. The next sign is the entire 2nd house, and so on around the wheel. One sign, one house, no fractions. If you have Scorpio rising, your 1st house is Scorpio, your 2nd is Sagittarius, your 7th is Taurus.

The advantage is that it's clean and it never leaves a planet stranded across a cusp. It also keeps the rulership chain intact, which is the part of traditional astrology that does the heavy lifting: every house has a sign, every sign has a ruling planet, and where that planet sits tells you how the house's subject actually goes.

What a chart is not
A birth chart is not a verdict. It doesn't say what will happen to you, and it doesn't say who you have to be. It describes conditions, tendencies, and the specific shape of your material.

It also isn't a personality quiz with twelve answers. You have all twelve signs in your chart and all twelve houses. The whole wheel is yours. What varies is which rooms are furnished, and which planets are sitting in them.

And it doesn't expire. Your chart is fixed at birth. What changes is the sky above it, which is a separate subject: transits, the ongoing conversation between the current sky and the map you were born with.

How to read yours, in order
1. Start with the big three. Sun, Moon, and rising sign. Identity, inner life, and approach.
2. Find your chart ruler. The traditional ruler of your rising sign, and the house it sits in. That house is the room your life keeps returning to.
3. Read the busy houses. Where are the planets stacked? That's where the volume is.
4. Notice the empty ones. Most houses are empty in most charts. Empty is not missing. Follow the house's ruler instead.
5. Then aspects. How the planets talk to each other, and which conversations are tense.

You don't have to learn it all at once. Read your Sun page, then your Moon page, then your rising sign. Everything else builds on those three.

Your chart is in TLDR Astro under Birth Chart. If your birth time is unknown, enter noon and treat the houses and the Moon's exact degree as approximate.

rows.headline: Your Sun, Moon, and rising sign
rows.summary: Most people meet astrology through one placement. Someone asks your sign, you say the month you were born in, and that's your Sun. It's real. It's also about a third of the picture.
rows.body:
Most people meet astrology through one placement. Someone asks your sign, you say the month you were born in, and that's your Sun. It's real. It's also about a third of the picture.

The other two are the Moon and the rising sign. Together the three get called the big three, and they're grouped for a reason. They answer the three questions you'd want answered about anyone before anything else: who they are, what they need, and how they come at a room.

The short version, before the long one:

- The Sun is identity and vitality. What you're here to be.
- The Moon is needs and moods. What you're like off duty, and what settles you.
- The rising sign is approach and body. How you arrive, and how people read you before you've said anything.

The Sun: identity and vitality
The Sun is the center of the chart the way it's the center of the solar system. It describes the part of you that's steady underneath the day, the thing you keep coming back to being, and the conditions under which you feel most alive.

It moves about a month through each sign, so everyone born within roughly four weeks of you shares it. That's the honest limit of a Sun sign. It's a real description of a certain kind of person. It's not a description of you alone.

One useful correction: the Sun isn't a costume you were issued. It's closer to a direction. Most people grow into their Sun sign slowly, and the parts that feel most like it often show up later than the parts that feel like the Moon or the rising sign.

The Sun also governs vitality, in the plain sense. When you're depleted, the Sun's sign and house describe what actually refills you, and it's usually more specific than rest.

The Moon: needs and moods
The Moon is the fastest body in the chart. It crosses a sign in about two and a half days and the whole wheel in about a month, which means it can differ between two people born the same morning in the same hospital.

It governs your inner life: how feeling arrives, how fast, how visibly, and what you do with it. It also governs need, which is the part people skip. Your Moon sign describes the conditions under which you feel safe enough to stop performing. Some Moons need quiet. Some need company. Some need a plan, or a body of water, or a locked door.

The Moon is what you were as a child and what you go back to when you're tired or frightened. If the Sun is the direction, the Moon is the baseline.

Because it moves so fast, the Moon is the one placement that genuinely depends on your birth time. Over a single day it travels far enough that a morning birth and a late-night birth can land in different signs. If your time is unknown, treat your Moon sign as likely but worth checking.

The rising sign: approach and body
The rising sign, also called the Ascendant, is the sign that was coming up over the eastern horizon at the moment and place you were born. Not where a planet was. Where the horizon was.

It governs your approach: the manner you lead with, the pace you move at, the first impression you don't get to choose. It also governs the body, which is why traditional astrologers read it for physical build, constitution, and vitality alongside the Sun.

And it does one thing neither of the others does. In whole-sign houses, the system TLDR Astro uses, your rising sign becomes your entire 1st house, and every other house follows in order around the wheel. Change the rising sign and all twelve rooms move. The house pages explain that in full.

The traditional ruler of your rising sign is your chart ruler, the planet that steers the whole life. Leo rising sends you to the Sun. Virgo rising sends you to Mercury. Wherever that planet sits is the room your life keeps returning to.

Why the rising sign needs the birth time
The Earth turns once a day. That means the entire zodiac rises over the eastern horizon in twenty-four hours, and a new sign comes up roughly every two hours.

So the rising sign isn't sensitive to your birth time. It's made of it. Two hours of error and you have a different rising sign, a different chart ruler, and twelve houses in different places.

This is why astrologers ask for the minute and don't let it go. The date gets you the planets. The place gets you the horizon. The time is what turns a list of placements into a map of a life.

If you don't have your time, you're not locked out. Enter noon, read the Sun and the planets by sign, and hold the Moon and the houses loosely. It's often worth asking a parent, checking your birth certificate, or requesting the long-form record from the state or country where you were born.

"I don't feel like my Sun sign"
Almost everyone says this at some point. There are four ordinary reasons, and none of them mean astrology has failed.

1. You're meeting your rising sign. Other people see it constantly, and most of us experience our own manner from the inside as simply how things are done. If a description feels wrong, read your rising sign before you throw anything out.
2. You're feeling your Moon. What you feel like is not always what you are. A Capricorn Sun with a Pisces Moon has a private life that no Capricorn Sun description will ever mention.
3. The Sun is somewhere specific. A Sun in the 12th house behaves nothing like a Sun in the 10th, even in the same sign. House changes the whole delivery.
4. You may not be that sign. Sign dates shift by a day or so from year to year. If you were born near a boundary, the only way to know is to run the chart with your actual date, time, and place.

There's a fifth reason that isn't about your chart at all. Pop descriptions of the signs are written to be quotable, and quotable usually means flattened. The sign pages in this set try to give you the working version instead, including the cost.

How the three fit together
Read them as one sentence rather than three verdicts.

The rising sign is the door. The Sun is the room you're building behind it. The Moon is what's in the room when the door is shut.

Say you have Libra rising, a Scorpio Sun, and an Aries Moon. People meet someone smooth, even-handed, reluctant to force anything. Underneath that is a person built for depth, privacy, and long commitment. And underneath that is a temper that arrives in a half second and wants out immediately. All three are you. They just work on different shifts.

When the three agree, you get a clear person who may lack range. When they disagree, you get range and a lifetime of feeling slightly mistranslated. Neither is better. They're different problems.

Day chart or night chart
One more thing the birth time gives you, and it's simpler than it sounds.

If the Sun was above the horizon when you were born, you have a day chart. If it was below, you have a night chart. Above the horizon means the top half of the wheel, the daylight side. Roughly, born between sunrise and sunset is a day chart, born between sunset and sunrise is a night chart.

This matters because the seven traditional planets split into two teams, called sects.

- The Sun's team, the diurnal sect: the Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn.
- The Moon's team, the nocturnal sect: the Moon, Venus, and Mars.

Mercury joins whichever team it matches by position, depending on whether it rises before or after the Sun.

In a day chart, the Sun's team is working in its preferred conditions and tends to operate more smoothly. In a night chart, the Moon's team is. The practical payoff is that the same placement can be markedly easier in one chart and harder in another. Saturn in a night chart is the classic example, and it's why the tradition held that a Saturn return is rougher going for night charts.

Sect is a traditional distinction that most modern astrology dropped. It's worth knowing because it's one of the few things that explains why two people with the same placement report completely different lives.

What to read next
1. Your rising sign page first, if you have your birth time. It sets the frame for everything else.
2. Then your Sun sign page, then your Moon sign page. Each sign page has a section for the big three.
3. Then the chapter on the planets and points, which covers the rest of what's in your chart and what each planet governs.
4. Then the house pages, once you want to know where all of it happens.

You don't need to learn the whole system to get something usable. Three placements and their houses will carry you a long way.

Your big three are at the top of your chart in TLDR Astro under Birth Chart. If your birth time is unknown, enter noon and treat the rising sign, the houses, and the Moon as unconfirmed.

rows.headline: The planets and points
rows.summary: A chart has about ten bodies in it and a handful of calculated points. That's the whole cast. Everything you'll ever read in a chart is some combination of those, the signs they're in, and the houses they fall in.
rows.body:
A chart has about ten bodies in it and a handful of calculated points. That's the whole cast. Everything you'll ever read in a chart is some combination of those, the signs they're in, and the houses they fall in.

This page is the cast list. What each one governs, how fast it moves, and what it means when it shows up somewhere specific in your chart.

One piece of grammar first, because it makes the rest easy. A planet is a verb. It's a function, not a character. The Sun shines. The Moon feels and needs. Mercury thinks. Venus values. Mars acts. Jupiter expands. Saturn limits. The sign tells you the manner. The house tells you the room. The chapter on birth charts covers that grammar in full.

The seven traditional planets
Traditional astrology works with seven visible bodies, the ones anybody could see with their own eyes for thousands of years before telescopes. These seven are the load-bearing structure, and they're the only bodies that rule signs.

Speed matters here more than people expect. The faster a planet moves, the more personal it is, because fewer people share your exact placement.

The Sun. Identity and vitality. About a month in each sign, a year for the full circle. The Sun is the center of the self, the steady thing under the day, and the source of vitality in the plainest sense. It governs recognition, the will, and the father in traditional readings. Where your Sun sits is where you're most yourself and most visible.

The Moon. Needs and moods. About two and a half days in each sign, about a month for the full circle. The fastest body in the chart and the most private. The Moon governs feeling, instinct, memory, the body's rhythms, what settles you, and the mother in traditional readings. It's what you are when nobody's watching.

Mercury. Thinking and communication. Weeks in a sign, and it never travels far from the Sun, so it's always in your Sun's sign or one of its neighbors. Mercury governs thought, speech, writing, learning, trade, travel, and every kind of exchange. It goes retrograde three to four times a year, which the chapter on retrogrades explains properly.

Venus. Love and value. About a month in a sign, longer when it retrogrades, and like Mercury it stays close to the Sun. Venus governs attraction, pleasure, taste, art, money, and the whole question of what you find worth having. It describes how you love and also what you're willing to pay for.

Mars. Drive and assertion. About six to eight weeks in a sign, and months longer in a sign it retrogrades through. Mars governs action, appetite, anger, courage, competition, and the ability to cut something off. Where Mars sits is where you push, and where you fight when pushed.

Jupiter. Growth and meaning. About a year in a sign. Jupiter governs expansion, abundance, belief, teaching, travel, and luck of the ordinary kind. Wherever Jupiter falls, things tend to get bigger, which is useful and occasionally too much of a good thing.

Saturn. Structure and limits. About two and a half years in a sign, with an orbital period of about 29.4 years. Saturn governs time, boundaries, discipline, authority, endurance, and consequence. It's the planet of the long build. Wherever Saturn sits is where things take longer and last longer.

Benefics and malefics, without the doom
Traditional astrology sorted four of those planets by temperament.

The benefics are Venus and Jupiter. They describe ease, growth, pleasure, and connection.

The malefics are Mars and Saturn. They describe friction, restriction, loss, and effort.

The Sun and the Moon sit outside the pairing as the two lights. Mercury takes on the character of what it's connected to.

Here's the part modern summaries get wrong in both directions. The malefics aren't punishments and the benefics aren't prizes. Mars is how anything gets cut, defended, or started. Saturn is how anything gets built to last. A chart with no friction in it produces a person with no edges. Meanwhile Venus and Jupiter can overdo it, and they do: Venus into avoidance and appeasement, Jupiter into excess and overpromising.

Sect changes the picture too. In a day chart Jupiter is the more helpful of the two benefics and Mars is the harsher of the two malefics. In a night chart it flips, and Venus and Saturn take those roles. The chapter on the Sun, Moon, and rising sign explains sect.

So read a malefic as a place that asks for work, and a benefic as a place that comes easily enough to be taken for granted. That's closer to how the tradition actually used them.

The modern outers
Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto were discovered after the telescope. They're real bodies and they're in your chart, and TLDR Astro places them. They rule nothing. Sign rulership in this system belongs to the seven traditional planets, and it stays that way, which keeps the rulership chain intact.

What makes them different is speed. They move so slowly that they describe a generation before they describe you.

Uranus. Change. About seven years in a sign. Uranus governs disruption, invention, independence, and the break from an established pattern. In a chart it shows where you refuse to be predictable and where your life resists a settled shape.

Neptune. Imagination and dissolution. About fourteen years in a sign. Neptune governs imagination, art, compassion, escape, and the blurring of an outline. It's where the edges go soft, which is where inspiration lives and also where illusion does.

Pluto. Power and transformation. Between twelve and thirty years in a sign, because its orbit is uneven. Pluto governs power, depth, compulsion, and the kind of change that doesn't offer to put things back. In a chart it's where you rebuild from the ground more than once.

Because everyone born within years of you shares the sign, the personal detail for an outer planet comes from its house and its aspects to your faster planets. An outer planet sitting on your Sun or Moon is personal. An outer planet in a sign you share with millions of people is a description of your cohort.

Chiron
Chiron is a small body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus on a lopsided path, so the time it spends in a sign varies a great deal. It's a modern addition, not a traditional one, and it rules nothing.

Astrologers read Chiron as a tender spot: the place where something went wrong early, stayed sore, and eventually became the thing you're unusually good at helping other people with. Treat it as a useful lens rather than a load-bearing part of the chart.

The lunar nodes
The lunar nodes aren't bodies at all. They're the two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path. Eclipses happen near them, which the chapter on moon phases and eclipses covers.

The North Node was called caput draconis, the dragon's head, and Rahu in the Indian tradition. It's the point of increase. The South Node was called cauda draconis, the dragon's tail, and Ketu. It's the point of decrease.

They're always exactly 180 degrees apart, so they sit across an axis, and in mean motion they always move backward through the zodiac. They spend about 18 months on an axis and take about 18.6 years to return to where they started.

Modern practice reads the South Node as the familiar groove, the thing you already know how to do, and the North Node as the unfamiliar direction that costs something to move toward. It's a growth model rather than a traditional technique, and it's worth holding lightly.

The angles
Four points are set purely by your birth time and place. They're the corners of the map, and they're described in full in the chapter on birth charts.

- The Ascendant, your rising sign, on the eastern horizon. Approach, body, and the start of the 1st house.
- The Midheaven, or MC, the highest point. Career, reputation, and public role.
- The Descendant, or DC, opposite the Ascendant. Partnership and what you meet in other people.
- The Imum Coeli, or IC, at the bottom. Home, family, and the private foundation.

The whole zodiac crosses the horizon every twenty-four hours, so the angles move faster than anything else in the chart. That's the entire reason the birth time matters.

What to do with this
Don't try to hold all of it. Read in this order.

1. Sun, Moon, and rising sign. Covered in their own chapter.
2. Your chart ruler. The traditional ruler of your rising sign, and the house it's in.
3. Mercury, Venus, and Mars. These are the personal ones, and they're where most day-to-day recognition happens.
4. Jupiter and Saturn. The long shape of growth and the long shape of limits.
5. The outers, by house. Then Chiron and the nodes, last, once the rest makes sense.

Each planet has a section on every sign page and every house page. Take one placement at a time and read both.

Every planet, point, and angle in your chart is listed in TLDR Astro under Birth Chart, with the sign, the degree, and the house for each.

rows.headline: The twelve houses
rows.summary: Signs tell you the manner of a thing. Houses tell you where it happens. If the planets are the cast and the signs are how each one plays the part, the houses are the twelve rooms of an actual life: your body, your money, your family, your work, the people you sleep beside, the reputation that arrives in a room before you do.
rows.body:
Signs tell you the manner of a thing. Houses tell you where it happens. If the planets are the cast and the signs are how each one plays the part, the houses are the twelve rooms of an actual life: your body, your money, your family, your work, the people you sleep beside, the reputation that arrives in a room before you do.

This is the layer most people skip, and it's the layer that makes a chart specific to you rather than to everyone born that week.

What a house actually is
The sky turns. Over twenty-four hours, the whole circle of the zodiac rises in the east, climbs overhead, sets in the west, and passes under your feet. A house is one of twelve divisions of that circle, measured from where you were standing.

Because the sky turns roughly one degree every four minutes, the houses move fast. Two babies born in the same hospital ninety minutes apart can have every planet in the same sign and a completely different arrangement of rooms. The first has Venus in the 10th and becomes known for their taste. The second has Venus in the 7th and builds a life around a partnership. Same planet, same sign, different address.

That's why astrologers ask for the birth time, and why the chapter on birth charts is blunt about it. The signs survive a missing time. The houses do not.

Whole-sign houses
There are several house systems, and they disagree about where the walls go. TLDR Astro uses whole-sign houses, the system used in Hellenistic astrology and still standard across much of the world.

The rule is short. Whatever sign was rising over the eastern horizon at your birth becomes your entire 1st house. The next sign in order is your entire 2nd house. The next is the 3rd, and so on around the wheel until you're back where you started. One sign, one house. No fractions, no cusps splitting a sign in two.

Scorpio rising means your 1st house is Scorpio from 0 degrees to 30 degrees, your 2nd is Sagittarius, your 7th is Taurus. Every planet in Sagittarius, wherever it sits in the sign, is in your 2nd house.

The payoff is that the rulership chain stays intact. Every house is a whole sign, every sign has a ruling planet, and that planet's position tells you how the house's subject tends to go. More on that below.

The twelve houses in order
Each house has a subject, an older name from the Greek tradition, and a type. The traditional names are worth knowing because they carry the original flavor, which is often bolder than the modern keyword.

1. The 1st. Identity, the body, and self-presentation. Traditionally the Helm, the place you steer from. Angular.
2. The 2nd. Money, worth, and values. Traditionally the Gate of Hades. Succedent.
3. The 3rd. Communication, learning, and everyday connections. Traditionally the Goddess. Cadent.
4. The 4th. Home, family, and private foundation. Traditionally the Subterranean. Angular.
5. The 5th. Creativity, play, romance, and self-expression. Traditionally Good Fortune. Succedent.
6. The 6th. Work, health, and daily routine. Traditionally Bad Fortune. Cadent.
7. The 7th. Partnership and one-to-one relationships. Traditionally the Setting. Angular.
8. The 8th. Intimacy, shared resources, and deep change. Traditionally the Idle place. Succedent.
9. The 9th. Belief, study, travel, and the bigger picture. Traditionally God. Cadent.
10. The 10th. Career, reputation, and public role. Traditionally the Midheaven. Angular.
11. The 11th. Friends, community, and long-term hopes. Traditionally Good Spirit. Succedent.
12. The 12th. Solitude, the unconscious, and the behind-the-scenes. Traditionally Bad Spirit. Cadent.

Each of these has its own page with the planets walked through one at a time. Read the ones where your planets actually are before you read the rest.

Angular, succedent, cadent
The twelve rooms are not all equally loud, and the tradition sorted them into three groups of four.

Angular houses are the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th. They sit on the four corners of the chart: rising, setting, overhead, underfoot. A planet here is at full volume. It acts, it shows, other people notice.

Succedent houses are the 2nd, 5th, 8th, and 11th. They follow the corners. Planets here work steadily and accumulate. Less immediate, more durable.

Cadent houses are the 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th. They fall away from the corners. Planets here are quieter and more internal, and traditionally were read as weaker in worldly terms. That's a statement about visibility, not about value. Plenty of the most interesting parts of a person live in a cadent house.

The planetary joys
Seven of the houses have a planet that traditionally rejoices there, meaning the house suits that planet's job. It's an old scheme and it's a fast way to remember what a house is about.

- Mercury in the 1st. The person awake, present, and about to speak.
- The Moon in the 3rd. Daily rhythm, siblings, neighbors, the short trip made often.
- Venus in the 5th. Pleasure, play, romance, and making things for their own sake.
- Mars in the 6th. Labor, illness, and effort. The house of hard use.
- The Sun in the 9th. Vision, belief, and the long view.
- Jupiter in the 11th. Friends, allies, and good fortune arriving through other people.
- Saturn in the 12th. Solitude, confinement, and what happens out of sight.

Notice the pattern. The benefics sit in the two good houses, Venus in Good Fortune and Jupiter in Good Spirit, the malefics in the two the tradition called difficult, Mars in Bad Fortune and Saturn in Bad Spirit, and the lights sit above and below in a way that matches sect. It's a tidy system, and it holds up in practice.

The houses that can't see the rising sign
Here's a piece of traditional logic that modern astrology mostly dropped. Signs relate to each other by angle, and some pairs form no angle at all. Those signs are said to be in aversion: they can't see each other.

Counting from your rising sign, the 2nd, 6th, 8th, and 12th houses are all in aversion to the 1st. From where you stand, they're blind spots. The tradition read that as one reason these four were the harder houses to handle: money, daily grind, other people's resources, and the hidden life are subjects you tend not to see clearly about yourself.

That isn't a curse. It's a description of a structural angle, and it's useful. If your chart has weight in those houses, the subject probably takes more deliberate effort to get a clear look at, and outside perspective tends to help more than usual. The chapter on aspects covers aversion in more detail.

Following a house ruler
This is the single most useful move in traditional technique, and it's how you read a house that has no planets in it.

Every house is a whole sign. Every sign has a traditional ruler. Find the ruler, find the house it sits in, and read the two houses as a sentence.

Say your 10th house is Pisces. Pisces is ruled by Jupiter. Jupiter sits in your 4th house. Your career and public role, then, keep routing back through home, family, and private foundation. Maybe you work from the house. Maybe the family business is the career. Maybe your reputation is built on being the one who takes care of people.

Do this for your 1st house first. The ruler of your rising sign is your chart ruler, and the room it sits in is the room your life keeps returning to.

Empty houses
Most of your houses are empty. There are about ten bodies in a chart and twelve rooms, so even a chart with clusters leaves most of the wheel bare.

An empty house is not a missing subject. You have a body, money, a home, and relationships whether or not a planet is parked in the relevant room. An empty house just means the subject isn't running on its own dedicated staff. Follow the ruler instead, and read the house it lands in.

The reverse is also worth saying. Three planets in one house means that subject is loud, not that it's easy.

What to read next
Look up your rising sign, then count forward through the signs in order and write down which sign owns each house. That list is your personal map of the twelve rooms.

Then read the house pages for the houses that actually have planets in them, and find your chart ruler. After that, the chapter on aspects will show you how those planets talk to each other.

TLDR Astro shows your house layout under Birth Chart, with each planet labeled by house. If your birth time is unknown, treat the house placements as unconfirmed until you can check it.

rows.headline: Aspects
rows.summary: A chart isn't a list of separate placements. The planets are in the same sky at the same time, standing at measurable angles to each other, and those angles are what turn a list into a life.
rows.body:
A chart isn't a list of separate placements. The planets are in the same sky at the same time, standing at measurable angles to each other, and those angles are what turn a list into a life.

An aspect is one of those angles. Two planets, a certain number of degrees apart around the zodiac, in a relationship the tradition considered meaningful. Everything else in the chart tells you what the parts are. Aspects tell you how they get along.

What an aspect is, mechanically
The zodiac is a circle of 360 degrees, divided into twelve signs of 30 degrees each. Every planet sits at a specific degree of a specific sign. Subtract one position from the other and you have the angle between them.

Mars at 12 degrees of Aries and Saturn at 14 degrees of Cancer are about 92 degrees apart. That's close to a square, so those two are in a square. Nothing more mystical than that is going on at the level of definition.

The classical set comes from Ptolemy, and there are five of them. Modern astrology invented a longer list of smaller angles. TLDR Astro works with the five major aspects, for reasons that will be clearer by the end of this chapter.

Ptolemy's five
Conjunction, 0 degrees. Two planets in the same place. They don't negotiate, they merge. Whatever the first one does, it now does through the second. A Venus conjunct Jupiter can't be generous without being warm about it. A Mars conjunct Saturn can't push without also braking. The conjunction takes its character from the planets involved, which makes it the one aspect that isn't easy or hard in itself.

Sextile, 60 degrees. Two signs apart. The signs share polarity and sit in cooperative elements: fire with air, earth with water. A sextile is workable. It's an opportunity that requires you to pick it up, which is the honest version of what people mean by "a good aspect." Nothing happens here unless you do something.

Square, 90 degrees. Three signs apart. The two signs share a modality, meaning they operate at the same tempo, and clash by element. Two cardinal signs both want to start, in incompatible ways. A square is friction that produces motion. It's the aspect most likely to show up as an actual problem you had to solve, and most likely to build something durable in the process.

Trine, 120 degrees. Four signs apart, same element. The two planets understand each other without translation. Talent lives here, and so does the thing you're good at and therefore never practice. A trine gives you the ability. It does not give you the discipline.

Opposition, 180 degrees. Six signs apart, directly across the wheel. The two signs share a modality and sit on one of the six axes, like Aries and Libra, self and others. An opposition is a see-saw. You tend to run one end at a time and then overcorrect into the other, and the resolution is not picking a side but learning to hold both. Oppositions often play out through other people, because the far end of the axis is easy to see in someone else and hard to see in yourself.

The sign logic underneath
Here's the part that makes aspects easy to remember. In whole-sign terms, aspects are relationships between signs first and exact degrees second.

- Same sign: conjunction.
- Two signs apart: sextile. Compatible elements.
- Three signs apart: square. Same modality, clashing elements.
- Four signs apart: trine. Same element.
- Six signs apart: opposition. Same modality, opposite sides of an axis.

That's why trines feel fluent and squares feel like work. A trine connects two signs built the same way. A square connects two signs running at the same speed in different directions.

Orbs
Planets are rarely at an exact angle. An orb is the allowance around exactness inside which the aspect still counts.

The principle is simple even though astrologers disagree about the numbers. The tighter the aspect, the stronger it works. A square that is nearly exact is a defining feature of a chart. A square at the edge of its allowance is a background detail. The traditional approach scales the allowance by planet, giving the Sun and Moon more room than Mercury or Mars, on the reasoning that the brighter body has a larger sphere of influence.

Practical advice: when you look at your own chart, sort the aspects by how close they are to exact and start at the top. The tightest two or three are doing most of the work.

Applying and separating
Planets move at different speeds, so an aspect is either forming or breaking up.

An applying aspect is one where the faster planet is still closing in on exactness. The tradition read these as the live ones, still gathering, with the outcome ahead of them.

A separating aspect is one where exactness has already passed and the faster planet is pulling away. These were read as settled, already spent, describing something that has happened rather than something arriving.

In a birth chart this is a matter of emphasis rather than a verdict, and an applying aspect tends to be the more insistent of the two. Where it really matters is with transits, where an applying aspect from the current sky is the one still building. The chapter on your chart and the current sky covers that.

Aversion: the signs that can't see each other
Two signs that form none of the five aspects are in aversion. They can't see each other. This is a real traditional category, and losing it is one of the things modern astrology gave up when it filled the gaps with minor aspects.

Two arrangements produce aversion. Signs next door to each other, 30 degrees apart, and signs five apart, 150 degrees apart. Modern practice calls these the semi-sextile and the quincunx and reads them as weak aspects. The tradition read them as no aspect, which is a stronger and more useful claim.

Aversion means the two planets have no line of sight. They're both in your chart and they operate without reference to each other. That explains things a list of aspects can't: the part of your life that never seems to communicate with another part, despite both being right there.

This is also why the 2nd, 6th, 8th, and 12th houses were treated as difficult. Counted from the rising sign, all four are in aversion to the 1st. The chapter on the twelve houses goes into that.

Hard is not punishment, easy is not free
The old vocabulary splits aspects into hard, meaning the square and the opposition, and soft, meaning the trine and the sextile. Useful shorthand, easy to misread.

A square is not something being done to you. It's two functions in your own chart that operate at cross purposes and have to be worked out in real time. People with tight squares tend to develop actual skill in the subject, because they had to. The cost is that it's tiring, and that the friction doesn't go away once you understand it.

A trine is not a free pass. It describes something that works without effort, which means you may never have built a method around it, and it can drift into laziness in exactly the area where you're most capable. The talent is real. The neglect is also real.

The planets involved matter more than the aspect category. Saturn trine Mars is still Saturn. Venus square Jupiter is still two benefics, and mostly shows up as overdoing the good thing.

How to read an aspect in your own chart
Take it in four steps.

1. Name the two functions. Not the sign names, the jobs. Mercury is thinking and speech. Mars is drive and assertion. Say each one in plain words first.
2. Name the angle. Merging, workable, friction, fluent, or see-saw.
3. Add the houses. An aspect always plays out in two specific rooms of your life. Mercury in the 3rd square Mars in the 6th is an argument between how you talk and how you work.
4. Check how tight it is. Close to exact means load-bearing. Wide means background.

Then say the whole thing as one sentence and see if it sounds like your life. If it doesn't, you've probably got the function wrong, not the geometry.

Aspects are the last layer to learn, and they should be. Read your Sun, Moon, and rising first, then the planets, then your houses. Come back here when the parts are familiar enough that the conversation between them means something.

TLDR Astro lists your aspects under Birth Chart, sorted by how close each one is to exact.

rows.headline: Your birth chart and the current sky
rows.summary: Your birth chart is a photograph. It was taken once, from one spot on Earth, at one minute, and it does not update. The sky inside it stopped moving when you arrived.
rows.body:
Your birth chart is a photograph. It was taken once, from one spot on Earth, at one minute, and it does not update. The sky inside it stopped moving when you arrived.

The real sky never stopped. Right now the Moon is somewhere. Mars is somewhere. Saturn is grinding through a sign it will be in for a couple more years. Those planets are still walking the same circle your natal planets are frozen on.

When a moving planet reaches the place where one of your natal planets is sitting, the two make contact. That contact is a transit, and it is most of what astrologers mean when they talk about timing.

Two layers. One fixed, one moving. That's the whole idea.

What a transit actually is
A transit is a planet in the current sky forming an aspect to something in your birth chart.

The aspects are the same five from the chapter on aspects: conjunction at 0 degrees, sextile at 60, square at 90, trine at 120, opposition at 180. Nothing new gets invented for transits. Same angles, same logic. The difference is that one of the two planets is moving and the other is not.

So if you were born with Venus at 12 degrees of Taurus, then transiting Saturn at 12 degrees of Aquarius is making a square to your natal Venus. Transiting Jupiter at 12 degrees of Virgo is making a trine to it. The natal Venus never moves. The visitor does.

Transits also happen to houses, not just to planets. A planet crossing into your 7th house is spending that whole stretch in the area of partnership, whether or not you have a natal planet there. Both readings are real. The house says what part of life is getting traffic. The natal contact says what in you is getting touched.

Why the same transit lands differently for two people
"Mars square Saturn this week" is a fact about the sky. It is not yet a fact about anyone.

Three things decide what a transit means for you specifically.

Which of your houses it crosses. Houses are set by your rising sign, so the same planet in the same sign lands in a different room for every rising sign. Saturn in Gemini is in the 1st house for Gemini rising and in the 7th for Sagittarius rising. One is a long look at yourself and your body. The other is a long look at your closest relationships.

Which natal placement it touches. A transit that hits nothing in your chart is faint. A transit that lands on your Moon, or on your Ascendant, or on your chart ruler, is not faint. Most of the sky's daily traffic passes over empty degrees in your chart and you feel very little of it.

What that planet already does in your chart. A planet rules the houses whose signs it governs, so transiting Venus is never just Venus to you. It is the ruler of two of your houses, dragging those subjects along wherever it goes. The house pages explain how to follow a ruler.

This is why two people can have the identical transit and describe two unrelated weeks. Neither of them is wrong.

Speed sets the register
How long a planet takes to cross a sign tells you what kind of event it can be. Fast planets make moods and appointments. Slow planets make chapters.

- Moon: about 2.5 days per sign. The texture of a day, not a life.
- Sun: about a month per sign. Where the light is this season.
- Mercury: a few weeks per sign, longer when it stalls and retrogrades.
- Venus: about a month per sign, longer across a retrograde.
- Mars: about 6 to 8 weeks per sign, months longer when it retrogrades there.
- Jupiter: about a year per sign.
- Saturn: about 2.5 years per sign.
- Uranus: about 7 years per sign.
- Neptune: about 14 years per sign.
- Pluto: anywhere from 12 to 30 years per sign, because its orbit is uneven.

Read that list as a volume knob. A Moon transit is a few hours of weather and then it's gone. A Saturn transit across your 10th house may be the two and a half years you changed careers. Uranus, Neptune and Pluto are slow enough that everyone born around the same time shares them, which is why they describe a generation better than they describe your Tuesday. They get personal when they sit on one of your own degrees.

Returns
A return is a moving planet arriving back at the exact degree it held in your birth chart. It has come the whole way around and found its own starting place.

The solar return happens once a year, near your birthday, when the transiting Sun reaches your natal Sun degree. It is the reason the birthday chart is a thing.

The lunar return happens about once a month, since the Moon crosses all twelve signs in roughly that time.

The Saturn return is the one people have heard of. Saturn takes about 29.4 years to go around, so it comes home at ages 27 to 30, again at 57 to 60, and a third time in the late 80s. Each one spans roughly 3 years, from Saturn's entry into your natal Saturn sign to its final exit, because Saturn usually retrogrades back over the same ground more than once.

What a Saturn return tends to produce is an audit. Structures that were built on someone else's terms, or on nothing, tend to come up for review: the job, the relationship, the city, the story you tell about your work. It can be a heavy stretch, and traditionally it asks more of a night chart than a day chart, for reasons the section on sect in the chapter on the Sun, Moon and rising sign covers. It is not a punishment. Saturn is not doing anything to you. You are roughly thirty, and the arrangements you made at twenty-two are being tested by a life that outgrew them.

Jupiter returns about every twelve years, since it spends roughly a year per sign. Those tend to read as openings rather than audits.

What transits are not
A transit is not a script. It does not tell you what will happen, and anyone who says otherwise is selling certainty, which nobody has.

Here is the honest version. A transit describes a condition and a pressure, not an event. Saturn crossing your 7th house is a period when partnership gets weighty and slow and real. Whether that means a marriage, a divorce, a long stretch alone or two years of therapy about it depends on you, your circumstances, and several thousand things no chart contains.

Transits also do not excuse anything. The sky is not responsible for what you said at dinner.

And a hard transit is not a sentence. Difficult contacts correlate with effort, friction and change, which is a description of most worthwhile periods of anyone's life. Knowing one is running may help you name what you're in the middle of. That's the actual value. Not prophecy. Context.

How to use the daily sky against your own chart
1. Open your chart first. Write down your Ascendant, your Sun, Moon and chart ruler, and the degree of each. The degrees are what let you spot a contact.
2. Look at today's sky. Note which sign each planet is in, especially the Moon.
3. Translate signs into your houses. With whole-sign houses this is easy counting. If Virgo is your 4th house, every planet in Virgo is currently in your 4th.
4. Check for contacts. Is any transiting planet within a few degrees of one of your natal degrees, or exactly square, trine or opposite it? Those are the live ones.
5. Weigh by speed. Slow planet on a personal point outranks a fast planet on nothing.

Start with the Moon for a week and see whether you notice it. Then watch one slow transit for a season. That is how the subject stops being theory.

TLDR Astro shows the current sky under Today, and your natal placements under Birth Chart. Open them side by side to see which of your houses today's planets are sitting in.

rows.headline: Retrogrades
rows.summary: A planet in retrograde is not moving backward. Nothing in the solar system reverses. What happens is that from where we stand, on a planet that is also moving, another planet appears for a while to be sliding back the way it came.
rows.body:
A planet in retrograde is not moving backward. Nothing in the solar system reverses. What happens is that from where we stand, on a planet that is also moving, another planet appears for a while to be sliding back the way it came.

Astronomers call this apparent motion. It is a trick of perspective, and it is completely predictable. Every retrograde for the next thousand years is already calculated.

Astrology does not claim the motion is real. It reads the appearance, the same way it reads a sunrise on a planet that is actually turning. What you get during a retrograde is a stretch of time when a planet covers the same degrees of the zodiac two extra times. That repetition is the whole subject.

The mechanics, plainly
Picture two cars on a long curved road, both going the same direction at different speeds.

When you pass a slower car, there is a stretch where it appears to drift backward against the landscape behind it. Neither car reversed. You simply moved past it. That is what happens when Earth overtakes Mars, Jupiter, Saturn or any planet further out than us.

Mercury and Venus sit between Earth and the Sun, so they do the passing. When one of them swings between us and the Sun, it appears to slip back against the signs for a few weeks before resuming.

Same road. Different speeds. That's it.

One traditional footnote worth having: for Mercury and Venus, the midpoint of the retrograde is when the planet sits at the exact heart of the Sun, a condition called cazimi, which the tradition treats as a moment of strength rather than weakness. The middle of the retrograde is not the worst part of it.

Shadow, station, direct
Three words do most of the work here.

Station. A planet appears to slow down, hold still against the background of signs, and then change apparent direction. It stations retrograde at the start and stations direct at the end. The stations are the slowest and most noticeable part of the cycle, because the planet sits on one degree for days.

Retrograde. The stretch between the two stations, when the planet is walking back over ground it already covered.

Shadow. The band of zodiac that gets crossed three times. Before the retrograde begins, the planet passes over the degrees it will later station direct on. That is the pre-shadow. After it stations direct, it has to re-cover the ground back to where it first turned. That is the post-shadow. Add them to the retrograde itself and you have the true length of the cycle, which is always longer than the dates people circle on a calendar.

Three passes over the same degrees. First pass, something comes up. Second pass, you go over it again with more information. Third pass, it gets settled or dropped.

Mercury retrograde
Mercury retrogrades 3 to 4 times a year. With shadow included, one cycle runs about two months, which means Mercury is somewhere in a retrograde cycle for a sizable share of any given year.

Mercury governs thinking, speech, messages, contracts, short trips and the moving of information from one place to another. During the retrograde, that traffic doubles back. Old conversations reopen. A message lands late or lands wrong. A decision you thought was closed wants another look.

The useful reframe is that Mercury retrograde is not a ban on doing things. It is a period biased toward review rather than launch. Re-write, re-read, re-check, re-connect. Sign the contract if the contract needs signing. Just read it twice and expect a clause to come back.

Venus retrograde
Venus retrogrades every 18 months for about 40 days. It is much rarer than Mercury and it lands harder.

Venus governs love, attraction, money, taste and what you consider valuable. During a Venus retrograde, people tend to reconsider those. Exes resurface. Relationships come up for honest assessment. What you thought you wanted turns out to be what you were used to. The plain advice is to postpone the permanent aesthetic decisions, which means the big haircut, the tattoo, the expensive redesign, and to let the reconsidering happen.

Venus also has the most beautiful pattern of any retrograde. Its retrogrades repeat in the same sign roughly every 8 years, and if you plot the positions of those meetings against the Sun over that period, they trace a five-petaled rose around the zodiac. The Babylonians tracked it. It is one of the reasons Venus has been considered a planet of harmony for as long as anyone has written astrology down.

Mars retrograde
Mars retrogrades every 2 years for 8 to 10 weeks, usually spanning two signs.

Mars governs drive, anger, competition and the ability to push. Retrograde, that push gets complicated. Effort goes into things and comes back out slowly. Anger turns inward or sideways instead of outward. Plans that needed force tend to stall, and starting a fight during this window often means fighting it twice.

It is a decent period for training, practice and preparation, and a poor one for declaring war on your landlord.

The outer planets
Uranus, Neptune and Pluto are retrograde for close to half of every year. So is Saturn, for a substantial stretch, and Jupiter too.

That number should defuse something. If a planet is retrograde nearly half the time, the retrograde by itself cannot be an emergency. It is the normal condition of the outer sky.

What matters with these is placement, not status. An outer planet retrograde becomes personal when it stations on one of your natal degrees, because a station means that planet sits on that exact spot for days or weeks, then crosses it again on the way back, then again going forward. Three passes over one point in your chart, spread across many months. That is the version you feel.

The panic, and the part that's real
Mercury retrograde has become a way to explain a bad week, and the internet made it a running joke. Both the panic and the joke miss the same thing.

Here is the honest position. Nothing is cursed. Your flight is not doomed. Technology does not know what Mercury is doing. Plenty of good things happen during retrogrades, including things that could only have happened because a delay bought someone time.

And also: people do consistently report the same textures during these periods. Mix-ups, returns, second looks, the past walking back in. Whether that is the sky or the well-documented human habit of noticing what we have a name for, the practical effect is the same, and the practical response is reasonable either way.

What actually helps:

1. Build in slack. More travel margin, more time before the deadline.
2. Confirm in writing. The retrograde version of a misunderstanding is expensive and boring.
3. Favor the re- verbs. Revise, repair, revisit, reconnect, return.
4. Do not stop your life. You cannot hold three months a year in reserve.
5. Watch what repeats. If the same subject comes back twice, it is worth your attention.

If you were born with a planet retrograde
Natal retrogrades are common, and they are not a defect.

A planet retrograde at birth tends to work inward first. The function still runs, but it runs through review, through a private pass, through a second look before it goes public. Mercury retrograde at birth often means someone who thinks it through before they say it and is more precise in writing than out loud. Venus retrograde can mean a private or unconventional way of relating to love and worth, arrived at rather than inherited. Mars retrograde often means the drive is real but indirect, with a longer fuse and a harder-to-see aim.

The Sun and Moon are never retrograde. They always move forward.

Read a natal retrograde as a note about direction of travel, not about strength. The planet's sign, house and condition still tell you most of the story, and the sign pages and house pages are where to go next for that.

TLDR Astro marks retrograde planets with an R in your birth chart and shows current retrogrades under Today.

rows.headline: The Moon's phases and eclipses
rows.summary: The Moon is the fastest thing in your chart and the only body that visibly changes shape. That shape is not the Moon doing anything. It's a geometry problem you can see with your eyes: how much of the lit half of the Moon is turned toward you, which depends entirely on where the Moon is standing relative to the Sun.
rows.body:
The Moon is the fastest thing in your chart and the only body that visibly changes shape. That shape is not the Moon doing anything. It's a geometry problem you can see with your eyes: how much of the lit half of the Moon is turned toward you, which depends entirely on where the Moon is standing relative to the Sun.

Everything in this chapter comes out of that one fact. The phases are angles. The eclipses are angles that line up more exactly than usual. Once you can see the mechanics, the rest stops being mysterious and starts being useful.

The lunar month
The Moon takes about 29.5 days to go from one New Moon to the next. That's the lunar month you feel. The Moon itself crosses all twelve signs faster than that, in about 27.3 days, roughly two and a half days per sign, and then spends the extra couple of days catching up to a Sun that has moved on.

The cycle has two halves.

Waxing runs from the New Moon to the Full Moon, the light growing each night as the Moon pulls ahead of the Sun.

Waning runs from the Full Moon back to the New Moon, the light shrinking as the Moon closes the distance from behind.

Two moments anchor the whole thing, and both of them are aspects you already know from the chapter on aspects.

The New Moon is a conjunction. Sun and Moon at the same degree of the same sign. The Moon is between us and the Sun, its lit face pointed away, so there's nothing to see. Traditionally this is also a Moon cazimi, meaning the Moon sits in the heart of the Sun, in the tightest possible contact with it.

The Full Moon is an opposition. Sun and Moon 180 degrees apart, facing each other across the wheel, which is why you see the Moon fully lit. It also means a Full Moon can never be in the same sign as the Sun. It's always in the opposite one.

That last point has a consequence people miss. Because the signs sit in six opposing pairs, every Full Moon of the year lands on one of six axes: Aries and Libra, Taurus and Scorpio, Gemini and Sagittarius, Cancer and Capricorn, Leo and Aquarius, Virgo and Pisces. During Leo season, the Full Moon is in Aquarius. During Pisces season, it's in Virgo. You can predict the sign of every Full Moon a year out with no software at all.

The eight phases, plainly
1. New Moon. Sun and Moon together. No visible Moon. The start of the count.
2. Waxing crescent. A thin curve appears in the evening sky as the Moon moves out ahead of the Sun.
3. First quarter. The Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun, a waxing square, and exactly half the disc is lit.
4. Waxing gibbous. More than half lit, filling out toward the opposition.
5. Full Moon. The opposition. The whole disc is lit and it rises as the Sun sets.
6. Waning gibbous. Past full, the light beginning to go.
7. Last quarter. 90 degrees the other way, a waning square, half lit again and rising after midnight.
8. Waning crescent. The last sliver before dark, visible before dawn.

The crescent and gibbous stretches are not aspects in the traditional five. They're just where the Moon happens to be on the way between the four that are. The four that count geometrically are New, first quarter, Full, and last quarter.

What people actually report is that the Full Moon is the loud part of the month. Things that were building become visible, and sleep gets worse for a lot of people. That's an observation, not a prediction. Your own notes over three or four months will tell you more about your pattern than any general rule.

What the nodes are
Before eclipses make sense, you need the nodes, because eclipses are entirely a nodal event.

The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to the path the Sun appears to take. Two orbits, slightly out of plane, cross at exactly two points. Those crossing points are the lunar nodes: the North Node, called caput draconis or Rahu in older texts and read as a point of increase, and the South Node, cauda draconis or Ketu, read as a point of decrease.

They are always 180 degrees apart, because they're two ends of one line. They move backward through the zodiac, spending about 18 months on each sign axis, and taking about 18.6 years to complete the full circuit. If you're around 18 or 19, or 37, or 56, the nodes are back where they were when you were born.

Most of the time a New Moon or Full Moon happens with the Moon a little above or below the Sun's path, so nothing is blocked. Near a node, the three bodies line up in the same plane, and one gets in the way of another.

Eclipses
An eclipse is a lunation that happens close enough to a node for shadows to fall.

A lunar eclipse happens when a Full Moon falls within 11 degrees 38 of a node. The Earth is between Sun and Moon, and the Earth's shadow crosses the Moon, which often goes a dim copper color.

A solar eclipse happens when a New Moon falls within 17 degrees 25 of a node. The Moon is between Earth and Sun, and it covers the Sun for a few minutes along a narrow strip of the planet.

These come in clusters. Eclipse season begins when the Sun comes within 17 degrees of a node, arrives roughly every 6 months, and runs about 34 days. That window is long enough to hold two eclipses, sometimes three, and then it closes for another half year.

Eclipses are intense, not omens
Ancient astrologers watched eclipses closely, and the records they kept are part of why we can calculate them now. In those texts an eclipse was usually read as a matter of state: kings, cities, harvests, wars. It was not about whether one person should sign a lease.

Modern practice reads eclipses as lunations with the volume up. The honest version is this. Eclipse periods often correspond with things moving faster than expected, news arriving, and decisions that were already half made becoming final. Endings cluster here, and so do beginnings. What you may notice is less control over the timing than usual.

What an eclipse is not is a verdict on you. It doesn't single anyone out, it isn't a punishment, and nothing about the geometry cares who you are. A shadow falls across a rock. The meaning lives in the house it touches in your chart.

The cost of eclipse season is a real one, so name it. Things decided quickly under an eclipse may need revisiting later, and a big move made at speed is still a big move. Slow down where you can. Some of it won't wait for you, and that's allowed.

Finding which house an eclipse lands in
This is the part that makes an eclipse yours rather than general.

1. Find the eclipse sign and degree. The app lists it, and so does any calendar of lunations.
2. Count houses from your rising sign. In whole-sign houses, your rising sign is the whole 1st house, the next sign is the whole 2nd, and so on. Count around until you reach the eclipse's sign. That's the house.
3. Read that house's topic. An eclipse in your 6th is about work, health, and routine. One in your 7th is about a partnership. The house pages have the full list.
4. Check for a natal planet nearby. If you have a planet within a few degrees of the eclipse, that placement is the one being lit up, and its function is the subject.
5. Remember the axis. Nodes come in pairs, so eclipse seasons work both houses of an axis for about 18 months. The 6th and the 12th move together. So do the 1st and the 7th.

If you don't know your birth time, you can still use the sign and any natal planets near that degree. What you lose is the house, which is the specific room. That's the same trade described in the first chapter.

What to read next
The chapter on your birth chart and the current sky covers transits in general, which is the larger category eclipses belong to. The chapter on aspects explains conjunctions and oppositions in more detail, since those are what a New Moon and a Full Moon actually are. And the house pages tell you what each of the twelve rooms covers, which is what turns an eclipse from a headline into something you can work with.

TLDR Astro shows each phase and eclipse in the daily sky, with the house it falls in for your chart.
